$15 an Hour Is How Much a Year? $31,200 Full-Time, Before Taxes

Direct Answer$15 an hour is $31,200 a year full-time before taxes — $600 a week, $2,600 a month. See part-time, overtime, unpaid leave, a federal-only take-home estimate.

Quick Answer

$15 an hour is $31,200 a year full-time before taxes — $600 a week and $2,600 a month.

The Short Answer: $31,200 a Year

At a standard full-time schedule — 40 hours a week, 52 paid weeks a year — $15 an hour equals $31,200 a year before taxes. That is the headline number, and every other figure in this guide is built from it:

Pay periodMathGross pay
HourlyYour rate$15.00
Daily (8 hours)$15 × 8$120.00
Weekly (40 hours)$15 × 40$600.00
Biweekly (80 hours)$600 × 2$1,200.00
Semimonthly (24 checks)$31,200 ÷ 24$1,300.00
Monthly average$31,200 ÷ 12$2,600.00
Annual (2,080 hours)$15 × 2,080$31,200.00

Figure 1: $15 an hour across every pay period, full-time schedule, before taxes and deductions.

Two cautions before you budget on $31,200. First, it is gross pay — taxes and deductions come out of it, and the take-home estimate later in this guide shows how much that matters. Second, it assumes a steady 40-hour week for all 52 weeks. Many $15-an-hour jobs do not guarantee that schedule, so the schedule table below shows what part-time hours and unpaid weeks do to the same rate.

What $15 an Hour Actually Means

An hourly wage is pay for each hour you actually work, while a salary is a fixed annual amount paid regardless of small week-to-week changes. Converting between the two is just a matter of counting hours — which is why the schedule matters as much as the rate.

$15 an hour sits in a distinctive spot in the U.S. pay landscape. It is more than double the federal minimum wage of $7.25 an hour, which has not changed since July 2009, and it is a typical starting rate in retail, food service, hospitality, warehousing, and entry-level customer service roles. For a job seeker, the practical question is rarely the rate alone — it is the rate times the hours you will actually be scheduled. A $15-an-hour offer at a guaranteed 40 hours a week is a $31,200 job; the same rate at an unpredictable 25–30 hours a week is a $19,500–$23,400 job. Always ask about the schedule before you compare offers by their hourly rate.

One more distinction that trips people up: the monthly figure. A month is not four weeks. Four weeks is 28 days, and only February in a non-leap year is that short. Multiplying a $600 weekly paycheck by 4 gives $2,400 — a number that, repeated twelve times, totals only $28,800 and silently deletes $2,400 of your year. The correct monthly average is always the annual figure divided by 12: $2,600.

The Formulas Behind the Number

Three inputs decide your annual pay at any hourly rate. Change any one of them and the answer changes:

InputFull-time standardWhat changes it
Hourly rate$15.00Your offer, raises, shift differentials
Hours per week40Part-time, reduced, or extended schedules
Paid weeks per year52Unpaid leave, seasonal shutdowns

Figure 2: The three inputs of every hourly-to-annual conversion.

Annual Gross Pay = Hourly Rate × Hours Per Week × Paid Weeks Per Year

Full-time: $15.00 × 40 × 52 = $31,200 per year

Payroll teams compress the last two inputs into a single baseline: 40 hours × 52 weeks = 2,080 hours, the standard full-time work year. The shortcut is simply rate × 2,080 — $15 × 2,080 = $31,200 — and it works in reverse too: divide any annual salary by 2,080 to get its full-time hourly equivalent. Our hourly-to-annual conversion guide walks through the baseline in full, including the 2,088-hour calendar quirk in years with an extra weekday.

Pay at Every Schedule: Part-Time to Overtime

The same $15 rate produces very different years depending on the schedule. These are the four schedules readers ask about most:

$15,600 / yr

Part-Time — 20 hrs/week

$300 a week, $1,300 a month on average. Half the full-time year, before taxes.

$23,400 / yr

Part-Time — 30 hrs/week

$450 a week, $1,950 a month on average. A common retail and food-service schedule.

$31,200 / yr

Full-Time — 40 hrs/week

$600 a week, $2,600 a month on average. The standard baseline for this guide.

$37,050 / yr

Full-Time + Overtime — 45 hrs/week

$712.50 a week: $600 regular pay plus 5 overtime hours at $22.50. Overtime is never guaranteed.

Unpaid time off works the same way, by cutting paid weeks instead of weekly hours. Each unpaid week at full-time costs $600: one unpaid week brings the year to $30,600, two unpaid weeks to $30,000, and four unpaid weeks to $28,800. Paid vacation, paid sick days, and paid holidays do not reduce the total at all — you are still paid for 52 weeks — which is why asking whether time off is paid is one of the highest-value questions in any $15-an-hour job offer.

Worked Examples: Four Real Paychecks

Each example follows the same Step / Math / Result pattern, so you can check every figure with a pocket calculator. All figures are gross, before taxes.

Example 1 — Full-time, 40 hours, 52 paid weeks

StepMathResult
Step 1 — Weekly pay$15 × 40 hours$600.00
Step 2 — Annual pay$600 × 52 weeks$31,200.00
Total$15 × 2,080 hours$31,200.00 / year

Example 2 — Part-time, 30 hours, 52 paid weeks

StepMathResult
Step 1 — Weekly pay$15 × 30 hours$450.00
Step 2 — Annual pay$450 × 52 weeks$23,400.00
Total$15 × 1,560 hours$23,400.00 / year

Example 3 — Full-time plus 5 overtime hours every week

StepMathResult
Step 1 — Regular pay$15 × 40 hours$600.00 / week
Step 2 — Overtime rate$15 × 1.5$22.50 / hour
Step 3 — Overtime pay$22.50 × 5 hours$112.50 / week
Step 4 — Annual total($600 + $112.50) × 52$37,050.00 / year
Total$31,200 base + $5,850 overtime$37,050.00 / year

Example 4 — Full-time with 2 weeks of unpaid leave

StepMathResult
Step 1 — Weekly pay$15 × 40 hours$600.00
Step 2 — Paid weeks52 − 2 unpaid weeks50 weeks
Total$600 × 50 weeks$30,000.00 / year

Honesty note: these examples assume every scheduled hour is paid at the stated rate. Shift differentials, tips, commissions, and holiday premium pay would change the totals, and overtime depends on eligibility and on hours actually worked over 40 in a single workweek — not on a monthly average. How $15 an Hour Compares

Small rate differences compound into thousands of dollars a year. This is why a $2 or $3 raise is worth negotiating hard at this pay level — $3 an hour is $6,240 a year at full-time:

Hourly rateAnnual gross (full-time)Gap vs $15/hrLimitation
$15.00 / hr$31,200—Gross, before taxes and deductions
$20.00 / hr$41,600+$10,400Gross; hours and benefits may differ
$23.00 / hr$47,840+$16,640Gross; schedule assumed identical
$25.00 / hr$52,000+$20,800Gross; tax bracket mix differs
$30.00 / hr$62,400+$31,200Gross; double the $15 annual figure

Figure 3: Full-time annual gross pay by hourly rate, 2,080-hour baseline. Gaps assume the same schedule.

Salary offers translate the same way. A $30,000 salary equals $14.42 an hour at full-time ($30,000 ÷ 2,080) — slightly less than $15 an hour — while a $35,000 salary equals $16.83 an hour. That conversion is the fastest way to compare an hourly offer against a salaried one: divide the salary by 2,080 and compare hourly rates, then weigh benefits and paid time off separately. Our wage guides for $20 an hour, $23 an hour, and $30 an hour use the identical method, so their figures line up with this one.

Gross Pay vs Take-Home Pay

$31,200 is what you earn, not what you keep. A rough federal-only sketch for a single filer in 2026 shows where the money goes — state tax, health premiums, and retirement savings would come out on top of this:

StepMathResult
Gross pay$15 × 2,080$31,200.00
Standard deduction (single, 2026)—−$16,100.00
Taxable income$31,200 − $16,100$15,100.00
Federal income tax10% × $12,400 + 12% × $2,700−$1,564.00
FICA (Social Security + Medicare)$31,200 × 7.65%−$2,386.80
Federal-only take-home$31,200 − $1,564 − $2,386.80$27,249.20 / year

That is about $2,270.77 a month or $524.02 a week before any state tax or benefits deductions. The federal brackets used here — 10% up to $12,400 of taxable income, then 12% — are the same 2026 brackets behind our $100,000 after-tax guide, and the 7.65% FICA rate is explained line by line in our FICA guide. Your own take-home will differ with your W-4, your state, and pre-tax deductions; run your exact numbers in the paycheck calculator rather than budgeting on this sketch.

Limitations

Keep these limits in mind before using any figure above as a budget:

  1. Gross, not take-home: every headline figure here is before federal, state, and local taxes, FICA, health premiums, and retirement contributions. The take-home sketch is federal-only and excludes state tax entirely.
  2. The 40-hour assumption is doing heavy lifting: irregular, seasonal, or on-call schedules produce lower annual totals. Budget on your average scheduled hours, not your best week.
  3. Overtime is conditional: the 1.5× rate applies to eligible non-exempt workers for hours over 40 in a workweek. Exempt salaried roles, some agricultural and transport jobs, and state-specific rules differ, and overtime hours can be cut at any time.
  4. Paid vs unpaid leave changes everything: two unpaid weeks cost $1,200 at this rate; paid leave costs nothing. Confirm which kind your offer includes.
  5. Tips, differentials, and bonuses excluded: night-shift differentials, tips, commissions, and bonuses are extra income that this guide does not count — and they are also not guaranteed.
  6. Not tax or legal advice: the 2026 federal figures are a planning sketch for a single filer with no credits or other income. Your return may differ; the paycheck tax guide covers the moving parts.

Frequently Asked Questions

The questions readers ask most about earning $15 an hour:

How much is $15 an hour per year?

At a standard full-time schedule of 40 hours per week and 52 paid weeks per year (2,080 hours), $15 an hour equals $31,200 per year before taxes. That breaks down to $600 per week, $1,200 every two weeks across 26 paychecks, and an average of $2,600 per month. If you take 2 weeks of unpaid leave, working 50 paid weeks instead, annual gross pay drops to $30,000.

How much is $15 an hour per month?

An average of $2,600 per month before taxes, calculated as $31,200 divided by 12 months. Do not estimate it as $600 a week times 4 weeks ($2,400) — most months are longer than exactly four weeks, and that shortcut undercounts your year by $2,400. The monthly average smooths out the calendar: some months you receive two biweekly checks and two months a year you receive three.

How much is $15 an hour biweekly?

A $1,200 gross paycheck every two weeks, for 26 paychecks a year. That is $600 a week times two weeks. Because there are 52 weeks in a year, not 48, biweekly pay produces two three-paycheck months each year — a useful rhythm for budgeting, since those extra checks are already part of the $31,200 total, not bonus money on top of it.

Is $15 an hour good pay?

It depends on your hours and where you live. At $31,200 a year full-time, $15 an hour is more than double the federal minimum wage of $7.25 an hour, and it is a common starting rate in retail, food service, and hospitality. But whether it covers your costs depends on rent, transport, and whether your schedule is a steady 40 hours — a part-time $15-an-hour job at 25 hours a week pays only $19,500 a year, a very different budget from $31,200.

How much is $15 an hour after taxes?

As a rough federal-only estimate for a single filer in 2026, about $27,249 a year. That figure subtracts $1,564 of federal income tax (on $15,100 of taxable income after the $16,100 standard deduction) and $2,386.80 of FICA tax from the $31,200 gross. State income tax, health premiums, and retirement contributions are not included and would lower take-home further — your actual paycheck depends on your W-4, your state, and your deductions.

What is $15 an hour with overtime?

The overtime rate is $22.50 an hour (1.5 times $15). Working 5 overtime hours every week on top of a 40-hour schedule adds $112.50 a week, or $5,850 a year, lifting gross annual pay from $31,200 to $37,050. Overtime is only paid on hours over 40 in a workweek for eligible non-exempt workers, and it is never guaranteed — so budget your essentials on the $31,200 base, not the overtime total.

Key Takeaways & Action Plan

  • $15 an hour is $31,200 a year full-time — $600 a week, $1,200 biweekly, $2,600 a month on average, before taxes.
  • Hours matter as much as rate: 30 hours a week pays $23,400, not $31,200 — always check the schedule behind the rate.
  • Monthly pay is annual ÷ 12: $2,600, not $600 × 4 — the four-week shortcut deletes $2,400 from your year.
  • Overtime lifts the year to $37,050 at 5 extra hours a week — but never budget essentials on overtime that can be cut.
  • Federal-only take-home is roughly $27,249 for a single filer in 2026 — state tax and benefits come out on top of that.
  • Next step: run your exact schedule in the hourly wage converter, then compare with our $20-an-hour guide to price your next raise.

Sources & Method

Figures are recomputed from the formulas in this article on the 2,080-hour full-time baseline. The federal-only take-home sketch uses 2026 federal rules consistent with the site's after-tax series: a $16,100 standard deduction for single filers, 10% on the first $12,400 of taxable income and 12% above it, and 7.65% FICA (6.2% Social Security plus 1.45% Medicare) — cross-checked against the $100,000 after-tax guide's brackets and the FICA guide's rates ($31,200 × 7.65% = $2,386.80). State income tax, credits, other income, tips, differentials, and bonuses are excluded except where a note says otherwise. This article is general information, not tax advice.
